stem: Which statement about the unconditional distribution of daily asset returns is a stylised fact?
correct: Its kurtosis is typically well above 3, so extreme moves are far more common than a normal model allows.
It has heavier tails than a normal distribution with the same variance.

distractors.text: Its kurtosis is typically below 3, because daily price moves are bounded by the size of the market.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the tail behaviour

distractors.text: Its kurtosis is almost exactly 3, because daily returns are sums of many small independent trades.
distractors.misconception: applies the central limit theorem to daily returns too naively

distractors.text: It is strongly positively skewed, because large gains are more frequent than large losses for equity indices.
distractors.misconception: reverses the typical skewness of equity index returns

distractors.text: Its tails are thinner than normal at daily frequency and become heavier only at the monthly horizon.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of the sampling horizon on tail weight

distractors.text: It is well described by a normal distribution, apart from a few data errors in the extreme tails.
distractors.misconception: dismisses heavy tails as measurement error

explanation: Daily returns are leptokurtic: sample kurtosis of 5 to 20 is common for equities, which is why normal VaR understates tail risk.

stem: Which pattern do volatility clustering and the serial dependence of returns display?
correct: Returns are nearly uncorrelated; squared returns are persistently autocorrelated.
Large moves follow large moves of either sign, so $|r_t|$ and $r_t^2$ have positive, slowly decaying autocorrelation.

distractors.text: Returns are strongly positively autocorrelated, while their squares are uncorrelated.
distractors.misconception: reverses which series carries the dependence

distractors.text: Squared returns have no autocorrelation, because uncorrelated returns are independent.
distractors.misconception: treats zero correlation as independence

distractors.text: Absolute returns are negatively autocorrelated at the first lag, since a large move is followed by calm.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the dependence in volatility wrong

distractors.text: Returns and squared returns are both exactly white noise, so volatility is constant over time.
distractors.misconception: ignores clustering of volatility

distractors.text: Autocorrelations of absolute returns die out within a day, so clustering is very short-lived.
distractors.misconception: understates the persistence of volatility

explanation: Returns are close to a martingale difference sequence, yet not independent: the conditional variance moves. The autocorrelations of $|r_t|$ stay positive for dozens of lags.

stem: What does the leverage effect describe?
correct: Negative returns raise later volatility more than positive returns of equal size.
Volatility responds asymmetrically, rising more after price falls.

distractors.text: Positive returns raise future volatility more than negative returns of the same size.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the asymmetry

distractors.text: Volatility responds identically to positive and negative returns of equal size.
distractors.misconception: describes a symmetric response

distractors.text: Traders borrow more when prices rise, so their margin accounts produce more volatile returns.
distractors.misconception: takes leverage literally as trading on margin

distractors.text: Returns are positively correlated with the change in volatility over the following day.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the correlation wrong

distractors.text: Volatility is higher on days when the trading volume is larger, whatever the sign of the return.
distractors.misconception: confuses the leverage effect with the volume-volatility link

explanation: The correlation between $r_t$ and later volatility is negative. Falling equity prices raise a firm's debt-to-equity ratio, one explanation for the name.

stem: How does the distribution of returns change as the horizon grows from daily to monthly?
correct: Tails become lighter and the distribution looks closer to normal, so kurtosis falls.
Aggregation over longer horizons moves the distribution toward normality.

distractors.text: Tails become heavier, because larger accumulated moves are possible over longer horizons.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of aggregation

distractors.text: The distribution stays exactly the same, since returns are identically distributed over time.
distractors.misconception: ignores that aggregation changes the shape

distractors.text: Volatility clustering becomes stronger, so monthly returns are more predictable than daily returns.
distractors.misconception: mixes up clustering with predictability of returns

distractors.text: The distribution becomes exactly normal for any monthly sample, whatever the daily dependence.
distractors.misconception: turns an approximate tendency into an exact result

distractors.text: Kurtosis rises in proportion to the number of days added.
distractors.misconception: confuses the growth of the variance with the behaviour of kurtosis

explanation: Aggregational Gaussianity: sums of dependent but weakly dependent returns approach a normal law (the excess kurtosis of an i.i.d. sum of $k$ terms falls like $1/k$). Dependence slows but does not stop this.

stem: Why are log returns often preferred to simple returns for multi-period analysis?
correct: The log return over several periods is the sum of the one-period log returns.
Log returns add across time, so a multi-period figure is easy to build.

distractors.text: Simple returns add across periods, while log returns multiply.
distractors.misconception: swaps which return is additive

distractors.text: A log return is exactly equal to the simple return for any size of price move.
distractors.misconception: ignores that they differ for large moves

distractors.text: Log returns cannot be below $-100\%$, so they are bounded below.
distractors.misconception: confuses log returns with simple returns, which are bounded by $-100\%$

distractors.text: Log returns are always normally distributed, whatever the asset.
distractors.misconception: attributes normality to the transformation

distractors.text: Log returns remove volatility clustering from the data.
distractors.misconception: believes the transformation removes dependence in volatility

explanation: $r_{t,t+k}=\ln(P_{t+k}/P_t)=\sum_{j=1}^kr_{t+j}$. Simple returns are bounded below by $-1$, while log returns range over the whole real line.

stem: In an ARCH(1) model $\varepsilon_t=\sigma_tz_t$ with $z_t$ i.i.d. $(0,1)$, what is the conditional variance of $\varepsilon_t$?
correct: $\sigma_t^2=\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}^2$, known at time $t-1$.
A function of the last squared shock: it varies but is predictable one step ahead.

distractors.text: A constant $\omega$ for all $t$, since the shocks have mean zero.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dependence on past shocks

distractors.text: $\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t+1}^2$, which depends on the next shock.
distractors.misconception: lets the variance depend on the future

distractors.text: $\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}$, which depends on the signed previous shock.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the previous shock enters squared

distractors.text: A random quantity with its own independent shock at each date, unknown at $t-1$.
distractors.misconception: describes stochastic volatility rather than ARCH

distractors.text: $\omega+\alpha\sigma_{t-1}^2$, which depends only on the previous variance.
distractors.misconception: describes a recursion without the squared shock

explanation: In ARCH the variance is a deterministic function of past shocks, which makes the likelihood easy to evaluate. Stochastic volatility has its own noise.

stem: Which conditions are needed for an ARCH($q$) model to have a positive conditional variance and a finite unconditional variance?
correct: $\omega>0$ and all $\alpha_i\ge0$ for positivity, and $\sum_i\alpha_i<1$ for the unconditional variance $\omega/(1-\sum\alpha_i)$.
Nonnegative $\alpha_i$ with positive $\omega$, and the $\alpha_i$ summing to less than one.

distractors.text: The $\alpha_i$ may be any real numbers, as the squared shocks are positive anyway.
distractors.misconception: ignores that negative coefficients can make the variance negative

distractors.text: $\sum_i\alpha_i>1$, so that the variance reacts strongly to past shocks.
distractors.misconception: reverses the stationarity condition

distractors.text: $\omega=0$, so that volatility is generated entirely by past shocks.
distractors.misconception: allows a zero intercept that would let the variance collapse to zero

distractors.text: The unconditional variance equals $\omega$, whatever the values of the $\alpha_i$.
distractors.misconception: forgets the amplification from past shocks

distractors.text: $\alpha_i\le0$, so that large shocks are followed by calm.
distractors.misconception: gives the wrong sign for the ARCH coefficients

explanation: With $\sigma^2=E\varepsilon_t^2$ stationary, $\sigma^2=\omega+\sum\alpha_i\sigma^2$, so $\sigma^2=\omega/(1-\sum\alpha_i)$, which needs $\sum\alpha_i<1$.

stem: An ARCH(1) model has normal innovations $z_t$. What is true of the unconditional distribution of $\varepsilon_t$ when its fourth moment exists?
correct: It has kurtosis above 3, so tails are heavier than normal even though $z_t$ is normal.
Mixing normal laws with changing variances produces excess kurtosis.

distractors.text: It is exactly normal, because each conditional distribution is normal.
distractors.misconception: confuses conditional with unconditional normality

distractors.text: It has kurtosis below 3, because the variance is bounded below by $\omega$.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the kurtosis effect

distractors.text: Its kurtosis equals 3, and heavy tails require non-normal innovations.
distractors.misconception: attributes all tail weight to the innovation distribution

distractors.text: It has the same kurtosis as $z_t$, since $\varepsilon_t$ is a scalar multiple of $z_t$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the multiplier $\sigma_t$ is random

distractors.text: It is symmetric but has infinite kurtosis for every positive value of $\alpha$.
distractors.misconception: overlooks the condition for the fourth moment to exist

explanation: For ARCH(1), $E\varepsilon^4/(E\varepsilon^2)^2=3(1-\alpha^2)/(1-3\alpha^2)>3$ when $3\alpha^2<1$. It is infinite when $3\alpha^2\ge1$.

stem: How are the parameters of an ARCH model typically estimated?
correct: By maximising a Gaussian likelihood numerically (QMLE).
By maximising a Gaussian likelihood numerically, which stays consistent for non-normal innovations.

distractors.text: By ordinary least squares on $\varepsilon_t$ in closed form, as in linear regression.
distractors.misconception: confuses a variance model with a mean regression

distractors.text: By setting $\alpha$ equal to the first autocorrelation of the returns.
distractors.misconception: confuses ARCH coefficients with return autocorrelation

distractors.text: By maximum likelihood based on the unconditional density, ignoring the order of the data.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dynamics that define the model

distractors.text: Only by the method of moments, because a likelihood is not available.
distractors.misconception: believes the likelihood cannot be written

distractors.text: Consistency needs the innovations to be exactly normal, otherwise estimates are inconsistent.
distractors.misconception: misses that Gaussian quasi-likelihood is robust

explanation: The conditional Gaussian log-likelihood is $-\tfrac12\sum\{\ln\sigma_t^2+\varepsilon_t^2/\sigma_t^2\}$. Standard errors need a robust (sandwich) form for non-normal innovations.

stem: How is Engle's LM test for ARCH effects carried out on the residuals $\hat\varepsilon_t$?
correct: Regress $\hat\varepsilon_t^2$ on $q$ of its own lags; $nR^2$ is approximately $\chi^2_q$ if there are no ARCH effects.
Test whether lagged squared residuals help predict the current squared residual, using $nR^2$ from that regression.

distractors.text: Regress $\hat\varepsilon_t$ on its own lags and test the coefficients, as for serial correlation.
distractors.misconception: confuses the test for ARCH with a test of autocorrelation in levels

distractors.text: Compare $R^2$ from regressing squared residuals on lags with the $t$ distribution with $n-q$ degrees of freedom.
distractors.misconception: misstates the null distribution

distractors.text: Reject the null of no ARCH when $nR^2$ is small, because lags then explain little.
distractors.misconception: gets the rejection region wrong

distractors.text: Fit an ARCH model first and test whether $\omega=0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the LM test with a test on the intercept

distractors.text: Apply the Ljung-Box test to the raw residuals; a significant value implies ARCH.
distractors.misconception: misses that ARCH shows in squared, not raw, residuals

explanation: Under $H_0$ the squared residuals are unrelated to their past, so $nR^2\to\chi^2_q$. A significant value means conditional heteroskedasticity.

stem: In a GARCH(1,1) model $\sigma_t^2=\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}^2+\beta\sigma_{t-1}^2$, when is the process covariance stationary?
correct: When $\alpha+\beta<1$, and $\alpha+\beta$ is called the persistence.
When the persistence $\alpha+\beta$ is below one, given $\omega>0$ and nonnegative $\alpha,\beta$.

distractors.text: When $\alpha<1$ and $\beta<1$ separately, whatever their sum.
distractors.misconception: checks each coefficient instead of the sum

distractors.text: When $\alpha+\beta>1$, so that shocks are amplified.
distractors.misconception: reverses the condition

distractors.text: When $\beta$ alone is below one, and $\alpha$ is unrestricted.
distractors.misconception: ignores the contribution of the ARCH term

distractors.text: When $\omega=\alpha+\beta$, so that the variance is balanced.
distractors.misconception: invents a balance condition

distractors.text: Always, since the variance recursion is linear.
distractors.misconception: assumes that linearity implies stability

explanation: Taking expectations, $\sigma^2=\omega+(\alpha+\beta)\sigma^2$, so finite $\sigma^2=\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$ requires $\alpha+\beta<1$.

stem: What is the long-run (unconditional) variance of a stationary GARCH(1,1) model?
correct: $\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$.
The intercept divided by one minus the persistence.

distractors.text: $\omega/(\alpha+\beta)$, the intercept divided by the persistence.
distractors.misconception: confuses one minus the persistence with the persistence

distractors.text: $\omega$, since the other terms have mean zero.
distractors.misconception: ignores the contribution of the lagged terms

distractors.text: $\omega/(1-\alpha)$, because only the shock term feeds the variance.
distractors.misconception: ignores the lagged variance term

distractors.text: $\omega(1-\alpha-\beta)$, so that more persistence lowers the long-run variance.
distractors.misconception: multiplies where it should divide

distractors.text: $\omega/(1-\beta)$, because $\alpha\varepsilon^2$ has mean $\alpha\sigma^2$ and cancels.
distractors.misconception: drops the shock term in error

explanation: With $E\varepsilon^2=\sigma^2$ and $E\sigma_t^2=\sigma^2$, $\sigma^2=\omega+\alpha\sigma^2+\beta\sigma^2$.

stem: How do multi-step variance forecasts of a stationary GARCH(1,1) behave as the horizon $h$ increases?
correct: Forecasts decay geometrically to the long-run variance at rate $\alpha+\beta$.
The gap to the long-run variance shrinks by $\alpha+\beta$ each step.

distractors.text: They stay at today's conditional variance for every horizon.
distractors.misconception: ignores mean reversion

distractors.text: They jump to the long-run variance after one step.
distractors.misconception: ignores the gradual decay

distractors.text: They grow without limit, as shocks accumulate.
distractors.misconception: confuses a stationary model with an explosive one

distractors.text: They revert faster the closer $\alpha+\beta$ is to one.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of persistence on the speed

distractors.text: They oscillate around the long-run variance with growing amplitude.
distractors.misconception: invents an oscillation with the wrong stability

explanation: $E_t\sigma_{t+h}^2-\bar\sigma^2=(\alpha+\beta)^{h-1}(\sigma_{t+1}^2-\bar\sigma^2)$. The half-life is $\ln(0.5)/\ln(\alpha+\beta)$ steps.

stem: How does a GARCH(1,1) model relate to an ARCH model?
correct: It is an ARCH($\infty$) with geometrically declining weights.
Past squared shocks enter with weights declining geometrically.

distractors.text: It is equivalent to an ARCH(1), since only one shock lag appears.
distractors.misconception: ignores the lagged variance term

distractors.text: The weights on past squared shocks increase with their age.
distractors.misconception: reverses the decay of the weights

distractors.text: Weights on all past squared shocks are equal, giving a long memory.
distractors.misconception: replaces geometric by flat weights

distractors.text: It has no memory of shocks beyond the previous period.
distractors.misconception: ignores the recursion through $\sigma_{t-1}^2$

distractors.text: It needs more parameters than an ARCH(10) model to describe the same memory.
distractors.misconception: reverses the parsimony argument

explanation: $\sigma_t^2=\frac{\omega}{1-\beta}+\alpha\sum_{j\ge1}\beta^{j-1}\varepsilon_{t-j}^2$. Three parameters give a long, smoothly declining memory.

stem: What characterises an IGARCH model, for which $\alpha+\beta=1$?
correct: Variance shocks never die out in forecasts, and there is no finite variance.
Forecasts never revert, and the unconditional variance is infinite.

distractors.text: Variance forecasts converge to $\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta)$, as in any GARCH model.
distractors.misconception: divides by zero

distractors.text: It has a finite unconditional variance, but forecasts converge more slowly.
distractors.misconception: confuses very high persistence with unit persistence

distractors.text: The returns become a random walk, so prices are non-stationary in mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses persistence of variance with persistence of returns

distractors.text: Conditional variance is constant over time.
distractors.misconception: confuses the unit-root case with no ARCH effects

distractors.text: The model cannot be estimated by maximum likelihood.
distractors.misconception: believes estimation fails at the boundary

explanation: With $\alpha+\beta=1$, $E_t\sigma_{t+h}^2=\sigma_{t+1}^2+(h-1)\omega$, so the forecast follows a line. RiskMetrics' exponentially weighted variance is an IGARCH with $\omega=0$.

stem: In the GJR-GARCH model $\sigma_t^2=\omega+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}^2+\gamma\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\mathbf 1\{\varepsilon_{t-1}<0\}+\beta\sigma_{t-1}^2$, what does $\gamma>0$ mean?
correct: Negative shocks raise next-period variance more than positive shocks of the same size.
The variance response to bad news is larger by $\gamma\varepsilon^2$.

distractors.text: Positive shocks raise variance more than negative ones.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the asymmetry

distractors.text: The model is symmetric in positive and negative shocks.
distractors.misconception: ignores the asymmetry term

distractors.text: Large shocks of either sign are given extra weight.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sign indicator with a size indicator

distractors.text: The model produces negative variance for some shocks.
distractors.misconception: forgets that $\alpha,\gamma$ are constrained to keep variance positive

distractors.text: The persistence of the process is unaffected by $\gamma$.
distractors.misconception: ignores that $\gamma$ enters the persistence

explanation: The indicator switches on the extra term after negative shocks. Persistence is $\alpha+\gamma/2+\beta$ for symmetric innovations.

stem: What is the main advantage of the EGARCH specification, which models $\ln\sigma_t^2$?
correct: No sign constraints are needed, since $\sigma_t^2=e^{\ln\sigma_t^2}>0$.
Modelling the logarithm keeps $\sigma_t^2>0$ automatically.

distractors.text: It models $\sigma_t$ rather than $\sigma_t^2$, so the variance stays symmetric.
distractors.misconception: confuses logging the variance with modelling the standard deviation

distractors.text: It requires all the coefficients to be positive.
distractors.misconception: imposes constraints that EGARCH removes

distractors.text: It is symmetric by construction, so it cannot capture the leverage effect.
distractors.misconception: ignores the sign term in EGARCH

distractors.text: It makes the conditional variance constant.
distractors.misconception: confuses a log specification with no dynamics

distractors.text: Its news impact is always a symmetric parabola.
distractors.misconception: describes GARCH(1,1) rather than EGARCH

explanation: $\ln\sigma_t^2=\omega+\beta\ln\sigma_{t-1}^2+\alpha(|z_{t-1}|-E|z|)+\gamma z_{t-1}$. A negative $\gamma$ gives a larger variance after bad news.

stem: What is the role of Student-$t$ innovations in a GARCH model?
correct: Heavier tails than normal, with finite variance if $\nu>2$.
Fat-tailed innovations; the normal is the limit $\nu\to\infty$.

distractors.text: They need $\nu<2$ for finite variance, which makes tails heavier.
distractors.misconception: reverses the condition for finite variance

distractors.text: They remove the need for volatility clustering to explain heavy tails.
distractors.misconception: believes fat-tailed innovations replace time-varying variance

distractors.text: As $\nu\to\infty$ they approach the Cauchy distribution.
distractors.misconception: confuses the limit with $\nu=1$

distractors.text: They make the conditional distribution thinner-tailed than the normal.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the tails

distractors.text: They make the conditional variance constant.
distractors.misconception: confuses innovation shape with the variance equation

explanation: Even GARCH with normal innovations leaves excess kurtosis in the standardised residuals; a $t$ law with $\nu\approx5$ to $10$ often fits better.

stem: What does the news impact curve of a volatility model show?
correct: How $\sigma_t^2$ depends on $\varepsilon_{t-1}$, other lags held fixed.
Next-period variance as a function of today's shock, past variance fixed.

distractors.text: The autocorrelation function of squared returns across lags.
distractors.misconception: confuses the news impact with the autocorrelation function

distractors.text: The way variance depends on future shocks in the data.
distractors.misconception: lets the curve depend on shocks not yet observed

distractors.text: A symmetric curve for every volatility model, including EGARCH and GJR.
distractors.misconception: ignores the asymmetry in these models

distractors.text: A straight line, since variance is linear in the shock.
distractors.misconception: ignores that variance is quadratic in the shock

distractors.text: The distribution of the standardised innovation.
distractors.misconception: confuses the news impact with the innovation density

explanation: For GARCH(1,1), $\sigma^2=\text{const}+\alpha\varepsilon^2$ is symmetric about zero. GJR and EGARCH tilt it so that negative shocks have more impact.

stem: Which comparison of volatility models is valid?
correct: A likelihood ratio test of $\gamma=0$ compares nested GJR and GARCH, while non-nested models like EGARCH and GJR are compared by information criteria.
Nested models can be tested by a likelihood ratio test, and non-nested ones can be ranked by AIC or BIC.

distractors.text: A likelihood ratio test can compare any two models, nested or not.
distractors.misconception: ignores the nesting requirement

distractors.text: The model with the larger log-likelihood is always better, whatever the number of parameters.
distractors.misconception: ignores the fitting penalty

distractors.text: GARCH and GJR cannot be compared because they use different data.
distractors.misconception: invents a data difference

distractors.text: EGARCH nests GJR, so a standard likelihood ratio test applies.
distractors.misconception: claims a nesting that does not hold

distractors.text: A model is better if it gives the larger $R^2$ for regressing squared returns on its fitted variances, and nothing else matters.
distractors.misconception: treats one evaluation metric as the only criterion

explanation: GJR reduces to GARCH when $\gamma=0$, so the LR test is valid (the null lies inside the parameter space). EGARCH and GJR are not nested.

stem: What is realised variance computed from intraday returns, and what does it estimate?
correct: The sum of squared intraday returns, estimating integrated variance.
$\sum r^2$, consistent for integrated variance without noise.

distractors.text: The sum of absolute intraday returns, which estimates the conditional mean.
distractors.misconception: confuses squared with absolute returns and variance with mean

distractors.text: The square of the daily return, which is an unbiased estimate of tomorrow's variance.
distractors.misconception: mistakes the daily squared return for the realised variance

distractors.text: A GARCH forecast of the next day's variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses a model-free estimator with a model forecast

distractors.text: The variance of intraday returns around their sample mean, divided by their number.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sum of squares with a sample variance

distractors.text: A consistent estimator of integrated variance for any sampling frequency, even with large noise.
distractors.misconception: ignores the effect of microstructure noise

explanation: Realised variance needs no volatility model: with continuous prices, $\sum r^2\to\int_0^1\sigma_s^2ds$ in probability as the interval shrinks.

stem: What is the effect of microstructure noise (such as bid-ask bounce) on realised variance computed at very high frequency?
correct: It biases the estimate upward.
Squared noise terms add to every return, so RV exceeds the truth.

distractors.text: It biases the estimate downward, because noise averages out in the sum.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the bias

distractors.text: It vanishes as the sampling frequency increases.
distractors.misconception: confuses the noise with discretisation error

distractors.text: It has no effect, since the noise has mean zero.
distractors.misconception: ignores that squaring makes noise add positive terms

distractors.text: It affects only the daily mean return.
distractors.misconception: assigns the effect to the mean

distractors.text: It biases the estimate by the same amount at every sampling frequency.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the number of noise terms grows with frequency

explanation: With noise variance $\omega^2$, $E[RV]\approx\int\sigma^2+2n\omega^2$, which grows with the number of returns $n$. Hence sparse sampling or noise-robust estimators are used.

stem: What does a volatility signature plot (average realised variance against the sampling interval) typically show?
correct: A stable level at moderate intervals, rising sharply at the finest intervals when microstructure noise is present.
Realised variance flat for intervals of several minutes, then climbing at tick frequency.

distractors.text: Realised variance that falls at the finest intervals as noise averages out.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of noise

distractors.text: A flat line at all intervals, which proves there is noise.
distractors.misconception: misreads a flat plot as evidence of noise

distractors.text: The autocorrelation function of daily realised variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses the plot with an autocorrelation function

distractors.text: Realised variance rising with the sampling interval, because longer intervals have bigger returns.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the sum of squares is stable if there is no noise

distractors.text: Trading volume plotted against the sampling interval.
distractors.misconception: confuses the variable shown

explanation: The rise at short intervals is the signature of noise: a plateau suggests an interval, such as 5 minutes, at which bias is small.

stem: What does bipower variation $\frac\pi2\sum|r_i||r_{i-1}|$ achieve?
correct: It estimates integrated variance robustly to jumps, so $RV-BV$ estimates the jump contribution.
Products of adjacent absolute returns are not dominated by a single jump, giving a jump-robust variance estimate.

distractors.text: It includes jumps in the variance estimate, just like realised variance.
distractors.misconception: forgets that products dilute a single jump

distractors.text: It estimates the microstructure noise variance.
distractors.misconception: confuses jumps with noise

distractors.text: It uses squared returns only, so it cannot be affected by jumps.
distractors.misconception: misdescribes the construction

distractors.text: $RV-BV$ estimates the continuous part of the variance.
distractors.misconception: swaps the continuous and jump parts

distractors.text: It is biased by the continuous part of the volatility and should only be used in the absence of volatility.
distractors.misconception: invents a bias that is not there

explanation: With a jump, $RV$ picks up the squared jump, while $|r_i||r_{i-1}|$ contains at most one large factor. The factor $\pi/2=1/(E|z|)^2$ corrects for $E|z|=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ under normality.

stem: What is the distributional behaviour of daily realised variance?
correct: It is strongly right-skewed, while its logarithm is close to normal.
Logs of realised variance are roughly Gaussian.

distractors.text: It is symmetric and close to normal, so modelling it in levels is natural.
distractors.misconception: ignores the strong skewness of realised variance

distractors.text: Its logarithm is more skewed than its level.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of the log transform

distractors.text: It can be negative on days of falling prices.
distractors.misconception: forgets that squared returns are nonnegative

distractors.text: It is white noise with no persistence.
distractors.misconception: ignores the strong persistence of volatility

distractors.text: Its logarithm is undefined because realised variance is often zero.
distractors.misconception: treats zero values as typical

explanation: RV is a sum of squares, hence positive and skewed; $\ln RV$ is nearly Gaussian and highly persistent, so HAR-type regressions on logs are common.

stem: Why is ordinary least squares applied equation by equation to a VAR($p$) model efficient?
correct: All equations share the same regressors, so joint estimation gains nothing.
With identical regressors OLS equals GLS.

distractors.text: The errors are uncorrelated across the equations, so GLS is unnecessary.
distractors.misconception: assumes zero cross-equation correlation

distractors.text: OLS is only valid if each equation has a different set of regressors.
distractors.misconception: reverses the condition

distractors.text: It is not efficient, and system GLS is always better.
distractors.misconception: ignores the identical-regressor result

distractors.text: Equations of a VAR cannot be estimated separately because they share parameters.
distractors.misconception: believes parameters are shared across equations

distractors.text: It requires the variables to be cointegrated.
distractors.misconception: confuses VAR estimation with cointegration

explanation: Zellner's result: seemingly unrelated regressions give no gain when every equation has the same regressors. OLS is then also the Gaussian MLE.

stem: What is the stationarity condition for a VAR($p$) model in companion form?
correct: All eigenvalues of the companion matrix have modulus less than one.
The companion matrix has all its eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle.

distractors.text: All eigenvalues have modulus greater than one.
distractors.misconception: reverses the condition

distractors.text: All entries of each coefficient matrix are smaller than one in absolute value.
distractors.misconception: replaces eigenvalues by entry sizes

distractors.text: At least one eigenvalue lies on the unit circle.
distractors.misconception: describes a unit root

distractors.text: All eigenvalues have negative real part.
distractors.misconception: confuses discrete-time with continuous-time stability

distractors.text: The determinant of the companion matrix is exactly zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses stationarity with singularity

explanation: Entries below one in size do not guarantee stability, for example $\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.9\\0&0.9\end{pmatrix}$ is stable, but $\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.6\\0.6&0.6\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $1.2$.

stem: What does it mean that $x$ Granger-causes $y$ in a VAR?
correct: Lags of $x$ improve predictions of $y$ beyond its own lags.
Past $x$ has incremental predictive power, tested by a joint $F$ test.

distractors.text: Changes in $x$ cause changes in $y$ through an economic mechanism.
distractors.misconception: confuses predictive content with structural causation

distractors.text: The contemporaneous correlation between $x$ and $y$ is nonzero.
distractors.misconception: confuses Granger causality with contemporaneous correlation

distractors.text: It implies that $y$ cannot Granger-cause $x$.
distractors.misconception: believes causality is one-directional by definition

distractors.text: The two series are cointegrated.
distractors.misconception: confuses predictive content with a long-run relationship

distractors.text: The test is based on a single $t$ statistic of the contemporaneous coefficient.
distractors.misconception: misdescribes the joint test on lags

explanation: Granger causality is about forecasting: it concerns whether the lags of $x$ add information. Feedback ($x\to y$ and $y\to x$) is possible.

stem: What is true of orthogonalised impulse responses in a VAR?
correct: They depend on the variable ordering, and die out for a stationary VAR.
Cholesky responses change with the order of the variables.

distractors.text: They do not depend on the ordering, because the innovation covariance matrix is fixed.
distractors.misconception: ignores the ordering dependence of Cholesky factorisations

distractors.text: They equal the coefficient matrices of the VAR directly.
distractors.misconception: confuses the impulse responses with the VAR coefficients

distractors.text: They never die out, even in a stationary VAR.
distractors.misconception: reverses the behaviour for a stationary system

distractors.text: Ordering matters only if the innovations are uncorrelated.
distractors.misconception: reverses the role of the correlation

distractors.text: They give the causal effect of a structural shock, whatever the ordering.
distractors.misconception: ignores the identifying assumption in the ordering

explanation: Cholesky imposes a recursive structure: the first variable responds contemporaneously to its own shock only. Different orderings are different structural assumptions.

stem: Why is the lag length of a VAR chosen carefully by an information criterion such as AIC or BIC?
correct: Coefficients grow like $k^2p$, and BIC penalises lags more than AIC.
Lags consume degrees of freedom fast, and BIC chooses shorter lags.

distractors.text: The number of coefficients grows linearly in $k$, so lag length hardly matters.
distractors.misconception: miscounts the parameters of a VAR

distractors.text: AIC penalises extra parameters more than BIC, so AIC chooses shorter lags.
distractors.misconception: reverses the penalties

distractors.text: The best lag length is always the longest feasible one, as more lags can only help.
distractors.misconception: ignores overfitting

distractors.text: The criteria are only available for univariate models.
distractors.misconception: believes the criteria do not apply to VARs

distractors.text: The likelihood alone suffices, as it never prefers over-parametrised models.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the likelihood rises with parameters

explanation: The penalty is $2/T$ per parameter for AIC and $\ln T/T$ for BIC, and a VAR($p$) has $k+k^2p$ mean and slope parameters per full system.

stem: What does it mean for two $I(1)$ series to be cointegrated?
correct: Some linear combination of them is stationary.
They share a common stochastic trend.

distractors.text: Both series are stationary, so any linear combination is stationary.
distractors.misconception: confuses cointegration with stationarity

distractors.text: Every linear combination is $I(1)$, so they drift together.
distractors.misconception: describes the absence of cointegration

distractors.text: The series are highly correlated in levels.
distractors.misconception: confuses correlation with cointegration

distractors.text: The two series have the same drift and the same variance.
distractors.misconception: replaces a stationarity property by matching moments

distractors.text: Their first differences are stationary, which holds for any two $I(1)$ series.
distractors.misconception: describes a property of all $I(1)$ series

explanation: For $y_t=\beta x_t+u_t$ with $u_t\sim I(0)$ and $x_t\sim I(1)$, the pair is cointegrated with vector $(1,-\beta)$. The vector is determined only up to scale.

stem: What is the problem of spurious regression?
correct: High $R^2$ and significant slope for unrelated random walks.
Unrelated $I(1)$ series look related, with misleading $t$ statistics.

distractors.text: The slope is never significant when the series are unrelated.
distractors.misconception: ignores the inflated test statistics

distractors.text: The residuals are stationary, so inference remains valid.
distractors.misconception: reverses the property of the residuals

distractors.text: The $R^2$ is close to zero for unrelated series.
distractors.misconception: reverses the behaviour of $R^2$

distractors.text: The problem disappears as the sample size grows.
distractors.misconception: believes more data cure the problem

distractors.text: It arises only for $I(2)$ processes, not for random walks.
distractors.misconception: misidentifies the order of integration

explanation: Granger and Newbold showed that with independent random walks the $t$ statistic diverges as $T\to\infty$, rejecting no relationship far too often.

stem: How does the Engle-Granger procedure test for cointegration?
correct: Regress in levels, then test the residuals for a unit root.
The null is no cointegration, with critical values differing from the usual ADF ones.

distractors.text: Test the residuals with the standard Dickey-Fuller critical values.
distractors.misconception: ignores that residuals are estimated and critical values shift

distractors.text: The null hypothesis is that the series are cointegrated.
distractors.misconception: reverses the null and alternative

distractors.text: Regress the first differences of one series on the first differences of the other and test the slope.
distractors.misconception: uses differenced series, which discards the long-run information

distractors.text: A rejection of the unit root in the residuals shows the series are not cointegrated.
distractors.misconception: reverses the meaning of rejection

distractors.text: It needs the cointegrating vector to be known in advance.
distractors.misconception: believes the vector must be pre-specified

explanation: The residuals are chosen to be as stationary as possible, so the ordinary ADF distribution is shifted; MacKinnon provides the proper critical values.

stem: In the VECM $\Delta y_t=\alpha\beta^\top y_{t-1}+\sum_i\Gamma_i\Delta y_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t$, what do $\alpha$ and $\beta$ represent?
correct: $\beta$ holds cointegrating vectors, $\alpha$ adjustment speeds.
$\beta^\top y_{t-1}$ is the error-correction term.

distractors.text: $\alpha$ holds the cointegrating vectors and $\beta$ the adjustment speeds.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of the two matrices

distractors.text: $\alpha\beta^\top$ must be full rank for the series to be cointegrated.
distractors.misconception: confuses the cointegrated case with a stationary VAR

distractors.text: $\beta^\top y_{t-1}$ is a unit root process in all cases.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the combination is stationary

distractors.text: The model is expressed in levels only and has no differenced terms.
distractors.misconception: ignores the differences on the left-hand side

distractors.text: $\alpha$ is unrestricted and $\beta$ identified with its scale.
distractors.misconception: drops the identification restriction

explanation: The rank of $\alpha\beta^\top$ equals the number of cointegrating relations. Rank zero gives a VAR in differences, and full rank gives a stationary VAR in levels.

stem: For $k$ series that are all $I(1)$, which statement about cointegrating relations is correct?
correct: At most $k-1$ independent cointegrating relations exist.
The rank lies between 0 and $k-1$.

distractors.text: There can be up to $k$ independent cointegrating relations.
distractors.misconception: allows the rank to equal $k$, which would imply stationarity

distractors.text: Rank zero means all the series are stationary.
distractors.misconception: reverses the interpretation

distractors.text: The cointegrating vector is unique, including its scale.
distractors.misconception: forgets the normalisation issue

distractors.text: The rank equals the number of unit roots in the system.
distractors.misconception: confuses the rank with the number of unit roots

distractors.text: The Johansen tests assume the cointegrating vectors are known.
distractors.misconception: misdescribes the Johansen approach

explanation: Johansen's trace and maximum eigenvalue tests are sequential: reject $r=0$, then $r\le1$, and so on. Unit roots number $k-r$.

stem: Which describes a linear Gaussian state space model?
correct: An unobserved state evolves by a state equation, and the observations are noisy linear functions of the state.
Observations $y_t=Z\alpha_t+\varepsilon_t$ depend on a hidden state with dynamics $\alpha_{t+1}=T\alpha_t+\eta_t$.

distractors.text: The state is observed directly and the noise comes only from the observation equation.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the state is latent

distractors.text: The measurement and state shocks are the same variable.
distractors.misconception: merges two separate noise sources

distractors.text: The state equation depends on future observations.
distractors.misconception: makes the state depend on the future

distractors.text: The model has no observation noise, so the data equal the state.
distractors.misconception: drops the measurement error

distractors.text: The state is always a constant over time.
distractors.misconception: confuses the state with a fixed parameter

explanation: Examples: local level, ARMA models in state space form and dynamic regression. The Kalman filter provides the optimal linear predictor of the state.

stem: What does the Kalman filter do at each time step?
correct: Predict the state, then correct it by the weighted prediction error.
A prediction step followed by an update with gain times innovation.

distractors.text: It uses only the latest observation and discards earlier estimates.
distractors.misconception: ignores the recursion

distractors.text: It runs backward through the sample to smooth the state.
distractors.misconception: confuses filtering with smoothing

distractors.text: The gain is independent of the variances involved.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the gain depends on the variances

distractors.text: The prediction step uses the current observation $y_t$.
distractors.misconception: moves information into the prediction step

distractors.text: It requires the states to be observed during estimation.
distractors.misconception: ignores that states are latent

explanation: Filtering gives $E[\alpha_t\mid y_1,\dots,y_t]$ and its variance; smoothing then uses the whole sample. In the Gaussian case these are exact.

stem: In the local level model, how does the Kalman gain depend on the variances?
correct: It rises with state uncertainty and falls with observation noise.
$K=P/(P+R)$, so noisier data get less weight.

distractors.text: It increases with the observation noise variance.
distractors.misconception: reverses the effect of the measurement noise

distractors.text: It is always one half.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dependence on variances

distractors.text: It can exceed one, so that the update overshoots the observation.
distractors.misconception: forgets that $K\in[0,1]$ in the scalar case

distractors.text: It does not depend on the state variance.
distractors.misconception: ignores the role of $P$

distractors.text: It is large when the measurement is very noisy, to correct the noise.
distractors.misconception: confuses the response to noise

explanation: With $K\to1$ the filter trusts the new data fully ($R\to0$); with $K\to0$ it ignores them ($R\to\infty$).

stem: What happens in the local level model once the state variance has converged to its steady-state value?
correct: An exponentially weighted moving average.
A fixed fraction of the error updates the level.

distractors.text: The state variance grows without limit.
distractors.misconception: confuses convergence with divergence

distractors.text: The filter becomes the simple average of all observations.
distractors.misconception: replaces the exponential weighting with equal weights

distractors.text: Weights on older observations increase with age.
distractors.misconception: reverses the weights

distractors.text: The filter equals the least squares linear trend fit.
distractors.misconception: confuses the filter with a deterministic trend regression

distractors.text: The gain is zero and the estimate stops changing.
distractors.misconception: ignores the state noise

explanation: Steady state: $\hat\alpha_{t|t}=\hat\alpha_{t-1|t-1}+K(y_t-\hat\alpha_{t-1|t-1})$ with constant $K$, the exponential smoothing recursion.

stem: How is the likelihood of a Gaussian state space model computed?
correct: From the filter's prediction errors $v_t$ and variances $F_t$.
By the prediction error decomposition, $-\tfrac12\sum\{\ln F_t+v_t^2/F_t\}$.

distractors.text: It needs the smoothed states from a backward pass.
distractors.misconception: confuses the likelihood with smoothing

distractors.text: It is computed directly from the true states, which are known.
distractors.misconception: ignores that states are latent

distractors.text: It has a closed form in the parameters, so no numerical optimisation is needed.
distractors.misconception: believes closed forms exist in general

distractors.text: It uses $F_t$ as the variance of the filtered state.
distractors.misconception: confuses the prediction error variance with the state variance

distractors.text: It is based on the unconditional distribution of each observation, ignoring dependence.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dependence between observations

explanation: The joint density factorises as $\prod p(y_t\mid y_{1:t-1})$, with $y_t\mid y_{1:t-1}\sim N(\hat y_t,F_t)$. Parameters are found numerically.

stem: What defines a Markov switching model?
correct: A latent regime follows a Markov chain and parameters depend on it.
The regime's next value depends only on its current value.

distractors.text: The regimes are observed, so the model can be estimated by regression on dummy variables.
distractors.misconception: ignores that regimes are unobserved

distractors.text: The regime at each date is independent of the previous regime.
distractors.misconception: removes the Markov dependence

distractors.text: The regime is a deterministic function of time.
distractors.misconception: confuses switching with a deterministic break

distractors.text: The regime depends on future regimes.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of dependence

distractors.text: The rows of the transition matrix need not sum to one.
distractors.misconception: ignores the property of a transition matrix

explanation: Examples: a bull and a bear regime with different means and variances. The transition probabilities $p_{ij}=P(s_{t+1}=j\mid s_t=i)$ are estimated with the other parameters.

stem: In a Markov chain regime model, what is the expected duration of regime $i$ with persistence probability $p_{ii}$?
correct: One divided by the probability of leaving the regime.

distractors.text: $1/p_{ii}$, one divided by the probability of staying.
distractors.misconception: confuses staying with leaving
gives the ratio of staying to leaving

distractors.text: $1-p_{ii}$, the probability of leaving.
distractors.misconception: reports the leaving probability instead of a duration

distractors.text: $p_{ii}$ periods, the staying probability.
distractors.misconception: confuses a probability with a time
invents a product in the denominator

explanation: The time spent is geometric with success probability $1-p_{ii}$, so its mean is $1/(1-p_{ii})$.

stem: How does the Hamilton filter update regime probabilities when a new observation arrives?
correct: Posterior $\propto$ the transition prior times the regime density at $y_t$.
Bayes' rule with a one-step transition prior.

distractors.text: The posterior equals the prior, ignoring the new observation.
distractors.misconception: ignores the data

distractors.text: It uses future observations to revise earlier regime probabilities.
distractors.misconception: confuses filtering with smoothing

distractors.text: The prior is the transition row of the single most probable previous regime.
distractors.misconception: replaces averaging by a hard assignment

distractors.text: Probabilities need not be normalised, since only ratios matter for decisions.
distractors.misconception: forgets that probabilities must sum to one

distractors.text: It only uses the regime densities and not the transition matrix.
distractors.misconception: drops the dynamics

explanation: Bayes' rule: $P(s_t=j\mid y_{1:t})\propto f(y_t\mid s_t=j)\sum_ip_{ij}P(s_{t-1}=i\mid y_{1:t-1})$. The normalising sum is the likelihood contribution.

stem: How do filtered and smoothed regime probabilities differ?
correct: Filtered uses data to time $t$, smoothed uses the whole sample.
Only filtered probabilities are available in real time.

distractors.text: Smoothed probabilities use only past data, and filtered ones use the future.
distractors.misconception: swaps filtering and smoothing

distractors.text: They are identical for all models.
distractors.misconception: ignores the role of future data

distractors.text: Smoothed probabilities are available in real time.
distractors.misconception: ignores that they need the whole sample

distractors.text: Filtered probabilities use the whole sample, including future data.
distractors.misconception: gives the information set of smoothing to filtering

distractors.text: Smoothing changes the model parameters, filtering does not.
distractors.misconception: confuses state inference with estimation

explanation: Smoothed regime dates are used in historical analysis such as dating recessions, while trading decisions must rely on filtered probabilities.

stem: Which feature complicates estimation of a Markov switching model?
correct: Regime labels are arbitrary and the likelihood can have several local maxima, so several starting values are used.
Relabelling the regimes gives the same likelihood, and the surface is often multimodal.

distractors.text: The likelihood is globally concave, so any starting value reaches the maximum.
distractors.misconception: assumes a concave likelihood

distractors.text: A single EM run is guaranteed to find the global maximum.
distractors.misconception: ignores local convergence of EM

distractors.text: The number of regimes is tested by an ordinary likelihood ratio test with the standard chi-square limit.
distractors.misconception: ignores the non-standard asymptotics

distractors.text: The regimes are identified by their order in time.
distractors.misconception: confuses labelling with temporal order

distractors.text: The model is not identified unless the transition matrix is the identity.
distractors.misconception: invents an identification condition

explanation: With two regimes, swapping the labels and the corresponding parameters gives identical fit. Testing one versus two regimes needs non-standard critical values.

stem: How is the spectral density of a stationary process related to its autocovariances?
correct: It is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance function.
Power at each frequency is a weighted sum of all the autocovariances.

distractors.text: It is the Fourier transform of the series values themselves.
distractors.misconception: confuses the periodogram with the spectral density

distractors.text: White noise has all its power at frequency zero.
distractors.misconception: reverses the shape for white noise

distractors.text: The spectral density can be negative at some frequencies.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the density is nonnegative

distractors.text: It equals the autocovariance at lag zero for every frequency.
distractors.misconception: confuses the density with the variance

distractors.text: It depends only on the mean of the process.
distractors.misconception: ignores the covariance structure

explanation: $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(\omega)d\omega=\gamma(0)$, so the spectrum decomposes the variance across frequencies.

stem: What are the properties of the periodogram as an estimator of the spectral density?
correct: It is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent.
Each ordinate is roughly $f(\omega)\chi^2_2/2$, so its variance does not shrink as $n$ grows.

distractors.text: It is a consistent estimator, so its variance falls like $1/n$.
distractors.misconception: believes more data reduce its variance

distractors.text: It is biased for every sample size and unbiased only in the limit of zero frequency.
distractors.misconception: misstates the bias

distractors.text: It equals the spectral density exactly at the Fourier frequencies.
distractors.misconception: treats a random estimate as the true density

distractors.text: It is just the sample variance repeated at each frequency.
distractors.misconception: confuses the periodogram with a scalar summary

distractors.text: It is consistent but biased, with the bias falling like $1/n$.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of bias and variance

explanation: Adding observations adds more Fourier frequencies rather than reducing the noise at each one. Smoothing or lag windows are needed for consistency.

stem: What is the effect of a wider smoothing window (bandwidth) when estimating a spectral density?
correct: It lowers variance but adds bias.
Averaging more neighbouring frequencies stabilises the estimate but blurs peaks.

distractors.text: It lowers both bias and variance, so the widest window is best.
distractors.misconception: ignores the bias-variance trade-off

distractors.text: It raises the variance but lowers the bias.
distractors.misconception: reverses the trade-off

distractors.text: It has no effect on the variance, only on the plot appearance.
distractors.misconception: ignores the averaging effect

distractors.text: It reduces the number of observations used in the estimate.
distractors.misconception: confuses bandwidth with sample size

distractors.text: It makes the estimate exactly equal to the true density.
distractors.misconception: treats smoothing as exact

explanation: Smoothing across frequencies averages roughly independent periodogram values. A narrow peak, such as a seasonal cycle, can be smeared out by a wide window.

stem: How does the sign of $\phi$ in an AR(1) process $x_t=\phi x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ affect its spectral density?
correct: Low frequencies for $\phi>0$, high frequencies for $\phi<0$.
$\phi>0$ peaks at frequency zero, $\phi<0$ near $\pi$.

distractors.text: For $\phi>0$ power is concentrated at high frequencies.
distractors.misconception: reverses the frequency concentration

distractors.text: The spectrum is flat for every value of $\phi$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the autocorrelation structure

distractors.text: The peak is at $\omega=\pi/2$ for any value of $\phi$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the AR(1) with a cyclical process

distractors.text: The spectrum does not depend on $\phi$, only on the innovation variance.
distractors.misconception: forgets the factor $|1-\phi e^{-i\omega}|^{-2}$

distractors.text: For $\phi<0$ the spectrum has a peak at frequency zero.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign wrong

explanation: $f(\omega)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi}|1-\phi e^{-i\omega}|^{-2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\pi}\{1-2\phi\cos\omega+\phi^2\}^{-1}$, largest at $\omega=0$ when $\phi>0$.

stem: A series contains a cycle with period $T$ observations. Where does it show in the periodogram?
correct: As a peak near the frequency $2\pi/T$.
At the Fourier frequency closest to $2\pi/T$ radians per observation.

distractors.text: As a peak near $T/(2\pi)$.
distractors.misconception: inverts the relationship between period and frequency

distractors.text: As a peak at frequency zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses a cycle with a trend

distractors.text: As a peak at the frequency $2\pi T$.
distractors.misconception: multiplies where it should divide

distractors.text: It does not appear, as the periodogram only shows the random part.
distractors.misconception: believes deterministic cycles are invisible

distractors.text: As a flat increase of power at all frequencies.
distractors.misconception: confuses a cycle with white noise

explanation: A sinusoid of period $T$ has angular frequency $2\pi/T$. If $T$ does not divide $n$, power leaks into neighbouring Fourier frequencies.
